Task and constraints: Find tree roots minimizing height in an undirected tree.
Idea: Repeatedly remove current leaves until only central vertices remain.
Technique and why it applies: Adjacency lists and degrees identify leaves; each layer removal updates neighbor degrees.
Invariant: The remaining one or two vertices are the tree center.
Edge cases: A singleton returns [0]; the input is guaranteed to be a tree.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space; no author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return center nodes that minimize a tree's height.
Idea: Peel leaves level by level until at most two nodes remain.
Technique and why it applies: Neighbor sets and a leaf frontier support successive pruning layers.
Invariant: Removing outer layers preserves the center of the tree.
Edge cases: A one-node tree returns [0]; valid-tree input ensures convergence.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space; no author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize coins earned by bursting all balloons in a chosen order.
Idea: Choose the last balloon burst inside each interval.
Technique and why it applies: Padded boundary ones allow dfs(i,j) to try each interior k and combine subinterval scores.
Invariant: dfs(i,j) represents the best score for balloons strictly between fixed boundaries.
Edge cases: Empty intervals score zero; lru_cache is used but not imported in the snippet.
Complexity: O(n^3) time and O(n^2) memo space; no author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize coins earned from bursting balloons.
Idea: Use bottom-up interval DP and try each possible last balloon.
Technique and why it applies: For each interval width, max_coins tests every interior index as the final burst.
Invariant: max_coins[left][right] stores the best score between retained boundaries.
Edge cases: Nonpositive values are filtered; standard balloon constraints are positive.
Complexity: O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Return the nth super ugly number from the supplied prime set.
Idea: Keep one heap candidate per prime and suppress duplicate values.
Technique and why it applies: Pop the smallest (candidate, prime-index), advance its index past seen products, then push the next product.
Invariant: The per-prime index points into the generated ugly sequence.
Edge cases: n=1 returns one; candidate duplicates are skipped using a set.
Complexity: Heap costs may make worst-case time O(nk log k), not O(nk); space O(n+k).

Task and constraints: Compute the nth number formed from allowed prime factors.
Idea: Keep a min-heap candidate stream for each prime and process tied minima together.
Technique and why it applies: Each emitted minimum advances all heap entries with that value and pushes their next products.
Invariant: Advancing every tied stream prevents duplicate values in the output sequence.
Edge cases: Several candidates may tie per output, up to the number of primes.
Complexity: Worst-case work can be O(nk log k), not simply O(n log k); space O(n+k).

Task and constraints: Find the nth super ugly number using a list of allowed primes.
Idea: Maintain the next multiple for each prime and select the minimum each round.
Technique and why it applies: Each output scans all primes and advances every stream equal to the minimum.
Invariant: The ugly sequence remains increasing, and duplicate candidates advance together.
Edge cases: n=1 returns one; prime streams that tie are all updated.
Complexity: O(nk) time and O(n+k) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Generate super ugly numbers using a heap of candidate multiples.
Idea: Pop one value and push products based on its first dividing prime.
Technique and why it applies: The heap starts with one and all primes; each iteration can push several products.
Invariant: The code does not deduplicate candidates, so repeated values may be counted more than once.
Edge cases: Duplicate heap entries can make the returned nth value incorrect.
Complexity: Time can reach O(nk log(nk)) and heap space O(nk); supplied O(k^2) space label is not general.

Task and constraints: Compute the nth super ugly number from allowed prime factors.
Idea: Use a min-heap with per-prime indices into the generated sequence.
Technique and why it applies: Pop the minimum and advance its prime index past entries attributed to later primes.
Invariant: ugly_by_last_prime tracks the prime index that generated each sequence value.
Edge cases: The skip rule is subtle and should be tested on small prime sets.
Complexity: Expected O(n log k) plus index advances; O(n+k) space. No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Count smaller later elements for each position in the array.
Idea: Scan right to left and use a Fenwick tree over bounded values.
Technique and why it applies: Offset each value, query the prefix below its coordinate, then increment that coordinate.
Invariant: The tree contains values already seen to the right of current index.
Edge cases: Offsetting supports negative values; querying only lower coordinates excludes equal values.
Complexity: O(n log U) time and O(U+n) space; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Count strictly smaller values to the right of each element.
Idea: Compress values and query/update a Fenwick tree while scanning right to left.
Technique and why it applies: Query the prefix before the current rank, save it, then add the current value.
Invariant: The tree contains only elements to the right, and smaller ranks exclude equals.
Edge cases: Repeated values share a rank and are not counted as smaller.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Count smaller later values using a binary search tree.
Idea: Insert from right to left; node counters record the number of smaller values in left subtrees.
Technique and why it applies: Queries add left-subtree counts while traversing right and return the count on equality.
Invariant: Each node's count summarizes smaller descendants beneath it.
Edge cases: Sorted input can unbalance the tree; equal values go right and are not smaller.
Complexity: Average O(n log n), worst O(n^2), space O(n); labels capture both cases.

Task and constraints: Count smaller elements to the right of each array position.
Idea: Use merge sort while carrying original indices and accumulating counts during merging.
Technique and why it applies: A smaller right-half value passing a left value increases that left index's count.
Invariant: Each segment becomes sorted while counts stay associated with original positions.
Edge cases: Equal values must not count as smaller; comparison order matters.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the lexicographically smallest subsequence containing each distinct character once.
Idea: Use a monotonic stack and pop larger characters that occur again later.
Technique and why it applies: remaining counts future occurrences; in_stack prevents adding a character twice.
Invariant: A larger stack top is removed only if it can be reinserted later.
Edge cases: Each character is pushed and popped at most once.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize the product of lengths of two words sharing no letters.
Idea: Encode each word as a 26-bit character mask, then compare pairs.
Technique and why it applies: A pair is valid when the bitwise AND of its masks is zero.
Invariant: A shared character sets a common bit; disjoint masks indicate no shared letters.
Edge cases: Repeated letters set the same bit; lowercase input is assumed.
Complexity: O(total characters+n^2) time and O(n) space; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize the product of two word lengths with disjoint character sets.
Idea: Sort words by length, encode masks, and prune pairs unable to improve the best.
Technique and why it applies: Nested loops test mask intersections and update the best product.
Invariant: Descending lengths make upper-bound pruning valid.
Edge cases: Sorting mutates the input list; repeated letters only set one bit.
Complexity: Worst-case O(n^2) pair checks plus character work; O(n) space. Combined label is not one tight bound.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum product of two words with no shared characters.
Idea: Bucket-sort by length, create masks, then test promising pairs with early stopping.
Technique and why it applies: The nested pair scan stops when remaining length products cannot beat the best.
Invariant: Descending length order justifies stopping the inner and outer scans.
Edge cases: Word lengths must fit the fixed 1000-bucket array.
Complexity: Worst-case O(n^2) time and O(n) space; claimed linear time only describes favorable pruning.

Task and constraints: Count bulbs remaining on after n rounds of divisor-based toggling.
Idea: Return the integer square root because only perfect squares have odd divisor counts.
Technique and why it applies: The code calls sqrt(n) and converts the result to int.
Invariant: Every non-square has divisor pairs; square roots create one unpaired divisor.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; sqrt is not imported in the shown snippet.
Complexity: O(1) time and space under the usual arithmetic model; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Count bulbs remaining on after n rounds of toggling.
Idea: Return floor(sqrt(n)), since perfect-square positions remain lit.
Technique and why it applies: math.sqrt computes the root and int truncates it for nonnegative input.
Invariant: Only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; math is explicitly imported.
Complexity: O(1) time and space; no author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Build the lexicographically largest length-k sequence from two arrays while preserving each source order.
Idea: Memoize recursive choices of the next largest feasible digit from either suffix.
Technique and why it applies: The helper searches both suffixes for their largest feasible digit and compares recursive continuations when digits tie.
Invariant: State (i,j,length) captures remaining suffixes and the number of digits still needed.
Edge cases: Equal leading digits require comparing full suffix results, which the code does with string max.
Complexity: Runtime can be large due to many memo states and suffix scans; storage also grows with cached strings. No labels supplied.
